primitives.name: Metamorphic Disease
primitives.verbatim_quote: The disease A in the parent does not necessarily appear, even when inherited, as A in the children.
primitives.assumptions: Genetic expression is not deterministic; phenotypic transformation occurs during transmission.

primitives.name: Mortality Immunity
primitives.verbatim_quote: Deaths by mere old age and the accompanying failure of vital powers without any well defined malady, are very common in my collection, but I do not find as a rule, that the children of persons who die of old age have any marked immunity from specific diseases.

primitives.assumptions: Death from senescence confers no protective genetic effect against specific diseases.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When mortality due to aging shows no hereditary influence on disease susceptibility.

layer2.mapping: Aging trajectory T is orthogonal to disease inheritance vector; immune states are not inherited.
layer2.telemetry: Correlation between parental longevity and offspring disease incidence

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight emerges from the interplay between inheritance mix and metamorphic disease. Each family's disease profile forms a complex vector in a multidimensional space, where proximity indicates shared genetic heritage. However, the transformation from parental to offspring disease types introduces non-determinism—this is captured by a probabilistic kernel K(A, A'). This kernel reflects the fact that even identical disease types in parents may manifest differently in children, complicating predictive modeling. The third primitive, mortality immunity, adds another layer: deaths from natural aging do not confer immunity, implying that senescence is decoupled from genetic disease resistance. These three primitives together define a triadic structure: inheritance mix defines the input space, metamorphic disease governs the transformation, and mortality immunity sets boundary conditions. The failure mode arises when these structures interact poorly—e.g., assuming deterministic inheritance leads to incorrect predictions, or ignoring the orthogonality of aging and disease susceptibility results in flawed risk assessment.
